title: Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit
subject: Funded Research Exclusion
summary: Fairchild Industries v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), is the leading federal appellate ruling on the R&D tax credit's funded research exclusion. For U.S. contractors, it holds research is not "funded" when payment is contingent on technical success and acceptance, because the researcher bears the financial risk of failure—regardless of progress payments or likely success.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural Posture and Factual Genesis

Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), modified Feb. 23, 1996, reversing 30 Fed. Cl. 839 (1994), stands as the foundational appellate authority in United States federal tax jurisprudence governing the "funded research" exclusion for the Research and Experimentation (R&D) tax credit. Decided by the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit before Circuit Judges Rich, Newman, and Schall, with Circuit Judge Newman authoring the opinion, the ruling reversed an earlier decision by the United States Court of Federal Claims that had denied Fairchild Industries, Inc. ("Fairchild") millions of dollars in research tax credits.

The controversy originated in July 1982, when Fairchild entered into a Fixed-Price Incentive (FPI) contract with the United States Air Force to design, develop, and manufacture the T-46A aircraft, designated as the "Next Generation Trainer" (NGT), a specialized aircraft intended to train Air Force pilots. The procurement contract was structured into two distinct operational stages: a Full-Scale Development (FSD) phase and a subsequent production phase. Under the FSD phase, Fairchild was obligated to develop and deliver two prototype aircraft and all necessary support systems. The production phase contemplated the manufacture of a target quantity of 15 additional aircraft. The R&D tax credit dispute centered exclusively on the qualified research expenditures incurred by Fairchild during the FSD phase.

The contractual architecture of the FSD phase was exceptionally stringent. The agreement incorporated over 1,000 pages of detailed technical specifications that required Fairchild to meet specific design, construction, quality, and performance standards. Furthermore, the Air Force imposed "Total System Responsibility" upon Fairchild, making the contractor responsible for the installation and integration of all NGT system elements, whether fabricated by Fairchild, its subcontractors or vendors, or furnished as government-furnished property. Financially, the FSD phase was subdivided into 11 separately priced contract line items (CLINs), subject to an amended FSD ceiling price of $133,485,885.

Between 1982 and 1986, Fairchild spent $216,056,000 on the FSD phase, approximately $82.57 million more than the amended FSD ceiling price; the Federal Circuit noted that Fairchild had incurred unrecovered research costs in excess of $95 million in the FSD phase. During the performance of the work, in accordance with Defense Acquisition Regulation (DAR) 7-104.35(a), the Air Force disbursed bimonthly refundable financing advances, termed "progress payments," calculated as a set percentage of Fairchild's actually incurred expenditures. In late 1986, Congress cancelled the T-46A program, and Fairchild and the Air Force agreed to termination-for-convenience terms. At the point of cancellation, the Air Force had disbursed $53.0 million in "liquidated" progress payments—advances applied against the purchase price of formally delivered and accepted line items—and $60.8 million in "unliquidated" progress payments representing advances for work-in-progress not yet formally accepted. A subsequent Air Force audit showed that Fairchild had successfully completed 90% of the FSD work and was entitled to payment of $120.6 million; the $53.0 million in liquidated and $60.8 million in unliquidated progress payments were applied to this obligation, and the remaining $6.8 million was paid.
The Taxpayer's Claim and the Internal Revenue Service Challenge

On its federal corporate income tax returns for the 1982 through 1985 taxable years, Fairchild reported $109.4 million in Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) attributable to its engineering activities on the T-46A FSD phase. Upon examination, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) disallowed approximately $19.6 million of the claimed QREs for reasons not related to the appeal, leaving a net balance of $89.8 million in otherwise eligible research expenditures.

With respect to the remaining $89.8 million, the IRS determined that 55.8% of the expenses—equating to $50.3 million—were ineligible for the tax credit because they had been "funded" by the Air Force within the meaning of Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 44F(d)(3). The IRS derived this 55.8% disallowance ratio by dividing the $120.6 million ultimately paid by the Air Force upon contract termination by the $216.1 million in total FSD costs expended by Fairchild. As a consequence of treating 55.8% of the research as funded, the IRS disallowed $5.8 million in R&D tax credits claimed by Fairchild for the 1983 and 1984 tax years; because of carryover and carryback effects, the disallowance affected only those two tax years.

Fairchild paid the assessed deficiency and initiated a tax refund suit in the United States Court of Federal Claims, contending that zero percent of its FSD research was "funded" by the Air Force because its right to retain any payment under the FPI contract was strictly contingent upon the technical success of the research and formal line-item acceptance by the government. Conversely, the Department of Justice (DOJ) and the IRS maintained that whether research is funded does not depend on whether the contract reserves to the government the right not to pay for unsuccessful research, that payment must be unexpected or surprising for the contractor to claim the credit, that the credit depends on the relative likelihood that the sponsor will pay, and that payment is the benchmark for determining whether the sponsor or the researcher is entitled to the credit.

body.text: Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The statutory provision adjudicated in Fairchild was enacted by Congress under the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA), Pub. L. No. 97-34, § 221(a), 95 Stat. 172, 241, codified originally as I.R.C. § 44F of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. Through subsequent legislative reorganization, the statute was redesignated: first as I.R.C. § 30 by the Tax Reform Act of 1984 (Pub. L. No. 98-369, §§ 471(c), 474(i)(1)), and then as I.R.C. § 41 by the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (Pub. L. No. 99-514, § 231(d)(2)). Under I.R.C. § 44F(a), a corporate taxpayer was entitled to a tax credit equal to 25% of the excess of its qualified research expenses for the taxable year over its base period research expenses.

To qualify for the credit under I.R.C. § 44F(d) (currently codified at I.R.C. § 41(d)), expenditures had to qualify as research and experimental expenditures under I.R.C. § 174 and survive three explicit statutory exclusions: first, qualified research conducted outside the United States; second, qualified research in the social sciences or humanities; and third, any research to the extent "funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or any governmental entity)," which was codified during the years at issue at I.R.C. § 44F(d)(3) and currently resides at I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H).

Because the Internal Revenue Code does not statutorily define the term "funded," the Department of the Treasury promulgated implementing regulations under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d), which was later redesignated in 2001 as Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) via T.D. 8930, 66 Fed. Reg. 280, 295. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(1) establishes the controlling legal test for whether contract research is "funded," stipulating that amounts payable under any agreement that are "contingent on the success of the research and thus considered to be paid for the product or result of the research (see § 1.41-2(e)(2)) are not treated as funding".

This regulatory architecture operates in tandem with Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2) as a set of "mirror image" rules designed to ensure that when two parties contract for research, the tax subsidy is allocated exclusively to the single party bearing the financial risk of research failure, preventing both double-claiming and the arbitrary destruction of the credit. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2), the customer or sponsor paying for the work may claim "contract research expenses" (generally 65% of the payments) only if the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, provides that research be performed on behalf of the taxpayer, and requires the customer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful. Conversely, if the agreement makes payment to the researcher contingent upon the success of the research, the customer is legally deemed to be purchasing a completed "product or result" rather than funding research; consequently, the customer is barred from claiming contract research expenses, and the researcher is entitled to claim its own in-house QREs.

Additionally, under the second prong of the funded research regulations—Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(2) (now Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2))—research is treated as fully funded if the researcher "retains no substantial rights in research under the agreement providing for the research". In Fairchild, the government did not contest that Fairchild retained substantial rights in the T-46A research, leaving the litigation focused squarely on the economic risk and payment-contingency prong of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(1).
The Trial Court Ruling and the Federal Circuit's Final Holding

In the initial proceeding, the United States Court of Federal Claims ruled in favor of the government, holding that Fairchild's research expenses were "funded" by the Air Force and disallowing the $5.8 million tax credit claim. The trial court reasoned that because Fairchild received bimonthly progress payments throughout the FSD phase, Fairchild "was spending the government's money to conduct the T-46A research, not its own" (30 Fed. Cl. at 850). Furthermore, the trial court concluded that although Fairchild argued it assumed the financial risk under the contract, "[t]he facts state otherwise" because Fairchild fully expected to be paid and ultimately received $120.6 million (30 Fed. Cl. at 849–51).

Subjecting the trial court's statutory and regulatory interpretation to plenary review, the Federal Circuit reversed. Judge Newman held that the Court of Federal Claims fundamentally misconstrued both the T-46A procurement contract and the regulatory framework of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(1). The Federal Circuit established that the statutory inquiry into "funding" turns strictly on who contractually bears the research costs upon failure, not on whether the researcher is likely to succeed or how the researcher finances its day-to-day cash flow.

Because the T-46A contract conditioned the Air Force's payment obligation on formal inspection and acceptance of each discrete line item against over 1,000 pages of technical specifications (DAR 7-302.2 and DAR 7-302.4), and mandated the repayment of all unliquidated progress payments if the contractor defaulted (DAR 7-104.35(h)), Fairchild remained legally at risk for every dollar of research expenditure until the work was successfully completed and accepted. Accordingly, the Federal Circuit held that Fairchild's qualified research expenses under the T-46A contract were not "funded" within the meaning of I.R.C. § 44F(d)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d), reversed the judgment of the Court of Federal Claims, and remanded the case to the Court of Federal Claims for further proceedings to determine the amount of Fairchild's qualified research expenses.
2. Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

While Fairchild ultimately prevailed at the appellate level, the protracted audit dispute, the initial disqualification by the IRS, and the adverse judgment in the Court of Federal Claims stemmed from specific contractual mechanics, financing structures, and interpretive vulnerabilities. Furthermore, subsequent federal appellate decisions applying the Fairchild standard—most notably Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023), and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. (MBJ) v. Commissioner, No. 23-1523 (8th Cir. 2024)—demonstrate how taxpayers routinely suffer complete R&D credit disqualification when their contracts and project documentation fail to replicate the exact legal safeguards present in Fairchild. A rigorous legal and technical dissection reveals five core evidentiary and contractual fault lines at the heart of the Fairchild doctrine.
The Financing versus Funding Fallacy: Mischaracterization of Progress Payments

The primary catalyst for the IRS's disallowance and the Court of Federal Claims' adverse ruling was the presence of $113.8 million in bimonthly progress payments ($53.0 million liquidated and $60.8 million unliquidated) disbursed to Fairchild prior to program cancellation. In examining the transaction, the trial court committed a fundamental analytical error: it did not distinguish statutory funding from the mechanics of financing, and so conflated the mechanics of cash-flow financing with the statutory allocation of funding risk. The trial court posited that a researcher only assumes financial risk if the researcher uses its own internal cash reserves or commercial debt to pay vendor bills and employee wages as the work proceeds, concluding that the receipt of government progress payments meant Fairchild "did not itself incur" the expenses (30 Fed. Cl. at 849–51).

The Federal Circuit dismantled this premise by examining the precise legal character of progress payments under federal procurement law. Under DAR 7-104.35(a), progress payments are disbursed based on incurred costs merely to provide working capital to defense contractors during multi-year engineering cycles. However, citing the Court of Claims decision in Marine Midland Bank v. United States, 687 F.2d 395 (Ct. Cl. 1982), and the Federal Circuit decision in Nuclear Research Corp. v. United States, 814 F.2d 647 (Fed. Cir. 1987), Judge Newman emphasized that progress payments are legally structured as refundable financing loans or advances secured by a priority government security interest in the contractor's inventory and work product, rather than partial purchases or unconditional compensation for services rendered.

Crucially, the contract's financing provisions stipulated that Fairchild had no right to retain progress payments unless the corresponding contract line items were delivered and accepted (DAR 7-104.35(a), (b)), and DAR 7-104.35(h) required all unliquidated progress payments to be repaid to the Air Force if the contract was terminated for default. In modern tax practice, a major evidentiary failure occurs when commercial contractors utilize milestone billing, percentage-of-completion invoicing, or progress draws without an express contractual clawback or refund provision. As confirmed by recent decisions such as MBJ v. Commissioner and Geosyntec, if a taxpayer bills a client via periodic invoices tied to incurred hours or project stages and is entitled to retain those interim payments even if the final deliverable fails to achieve its technical objectives, the payments are not financing advances; instead, they constitute fatal third-party "funding" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H).
Probability of Technical Success versus Legal Allocation of Risk Upon Failure

A second major point of contention in Fairchild was the government's assertion that the research credit is unavailable whenever a contractor possesses a high engineering probability of succeeding and fully expects to be compensated. The government argued that payment must be unexpected or surprising for the contractor to claim the credit and that the credit should be available only under unusually risky and uncertain fixed-price incentive contracts, while the Court of Federal Claims based its ruling on the likelihood that the Air Force would pay and on Fairchild's expectation of payment.

The Federal Circuit rejected this subjective probability standard as wholly unsupported by the text of I.R.C. § 44F or Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(1). The court clarified that the regulatory phrase "contingent on the success of the research" does not measure the magnitude of technological doubt or the statistical likelihood of default; rather, it strictly evaluates the legal consequence of technical failure. Even if an experienced aerospace prime contractor has a 95% probability of successfully engineering a prototype, the research is not "funded" so long as the contract dictates that if the research fails to meet specifications, the contractor bears the financial loss and receives no compensation for the failed deliverable.

However, taxpayers frequently misinterpret this aspect of Fairchild by committing the inverse error: arguing that any fixed-price or capped-fee contract is inherently risky and therefore un-funded. In Geosyntec (11th Cir. 2015), Grigsby (5th Cir. 2023), and MBJ (8th Cir. 2024), taxpayers contended that because their compensation was subject to a fixed price or a maximum cost ceiling, they bore the financial risk of exceeding their internal budgets or incurring cost overruns. The appellate courts uniformly rejected this argument, establishing a vital distinction between cost-of-performance risk—the economic risk that performing the contract will cost more than the fixed price or cap—and contingency-of-success risk, which is the legal risk of receiving no payment at all, or having to refund progress payments, if the research fails to produce the specified technical result. While Fairchild absorbed over $82.5 million in cost overruns ($216.1 million spent versus a $133.5 million ceiling), those overruns were not the dispositive legal reason Fairchild won; Fairchild prevailed because even the initial $133.5 million contract price was legally contingent upon delivering conforming prototypes under DAR 7-302.2 and DAR 7-302.4.
Granularity of Technical Specifications and Line-Item Acceptance Mechanics

A critical evidentiary distinction separating Fairchild from subsequent taxpayer defeats lies in the extraordinary specificity of the T-46A contract's technical acceptance criteria and default remedies. In Fairchild, the Federal Circuit highlighted four interlocking contractual mechanisms that proved payment was contingent on research success. First, the contract incorporated over 1,000 pages of explicit technical specifications governing design, construction, quality, and flight performance. Second, the agreement imposed "Total System Responsibility," contractually binding Fairchild to guarantee the functional integration of all NGT elements and preventing the contractor from blaming subsystem incompatibilities on the government. Third, under DAR 7-302.2 (Payments) and DAR 7-302.4 (Inspection and Acceptance), the Air Force was obligated to pay only if the deliverables satisfied the contract specifications; if any work was deemed technically unacceptable, the Air Force possessed the unilateral contractual authority to reject the work outright, compel Fairchild to correct the defective engineering at Fairchild's sole expense without increasing the contract price, or accept the non-conforming work subject to an equitable price reduction. Fourth, the FSD phase was divided into 11 separately priced CLINs, ensuring that Fairchild "remained at risk for each line item until the research was successfully completed and the product of the research was accepted".

When modern taxpayers face IRS disallowance under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), their primary documentary deficiency is the absence of these four mechanisms. For example, in MBJ v. Commissioner, the Eighth Circuit emphasized that while the structural engineering firm's contracts contained general review provisions, they "lacked the specificity of those in Fairchild Industries". Similarly, in Grigsby, the Fifth Circuit held that taxpayers cannot conflate ordinary commercial "contracts for products or services" with agreements where payment is expressly contingent on research success. Conversely, in Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, No. 7805-16 (T.C. Nov. 19, 2020), the Tax Court relied on Fairchild to uphold the taxpayer's R&D credits precisely because the fixed-price contracts included formal "quality assurance procedures, specific barometers for success, and mechanisms for inspection, evaluation, and acceptance". Without explicit contractual barometers defining technical success and granting the customer the right to reject deliverables and withhold or claw back payment for technical failure, a contract will be deemed funded.
Retrospective "Wait-and-See" Accounting versus Ex-Ante Incentive Certainty

During the Fairchild litigation, the IRS advanced an aggressive interpretation of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(5) (the "wait-and-see" rule, now Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(5)), which addresses situations where a taxpayer cannot determine at the end of the taxable year whether or to what extent research is funded. The government argued that the availability of the credit could not be decided until the project was over and the magnitude of the researcher's risk of nonpayment was known, and that if research was arguably close to the line of not funded, the taxpayer had to pay the full tax and wait and see whether the customer chose to pay for the research.

The Federal Circuit rejected this retrospective disallowance model, holding that the wait-and-see regulation applies only when the precise extent of funding cannot be determined at the time the return is filed (for example, in joint-venture situations), that it had no impact on Fairchild's contract because the contract expressly authorized the government to decline payment if the research was not successful, and that the government's theory contravened the core legislative intent of ERTA 1981. Quoting the House Ways and Means Committee Report (H.R. Rep. No. 97-201), Judge Newman observed that Congress enacted the research credit to "overcome the resistance of many businesses to bear the significant costs of staffing, supplies, and certain computer charges which must be incurred in initiating or expanding research programs". For a tax credit to function as an effective economic incentive when corporate executives make capital allocation decisions, "the tax credit must be a known factor when making decisions to commit money to research".

The court noted that this ex-ante certainty requirement is reinforced by the mirror-image regulation at Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(i), which mandates that a contract research agreement be "entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research". Under the IRS's flawed reading of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(5), a contractor operating under a contingent-payment agreement would paradoxically lose the tax credit if its research succeeded and the customer paid for the product, while retaining the credit only if the research failed and the customer refused to pay. While the Federal Circuit defeated this retrospective trap in Fairchild, taxpayers still trigger audit disqualifications under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(5) when they perform research under informal letters of intent, execute retroactive contract modifications that guarantee reimbursement of already-incurred costs, or fail to document the risk allocation prior to commencing engineering activities.
Interaction with the Substantial Rights Prong and Holistic Contract Review

Although the government conceded the "substantial rights" prong in Fairchild, subsequent jurisprudence—beginning with Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000)—demonstrates that satisfying Fairchild's economic risk test is only half of the statutory battle under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(2) and (3) (now Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and (3)), even if a researcher bears 100% of the financial risk under a strict Fairchild-compliant fixed-price contract, the research is treated as fully funded if the researcher "retains no substantial rights in research under the agreement".

As established in Lockheed Martin and enforced in IRS audit directives, a researcher retains substantial rights if it maintains the legal right to use or exploit the results of the research in its trade or business without having to pay a royalty or fee to the customer, even if that right is non-exclusive. Conversely, "incidental benefits" such as increased engineering experience or general technical know-how do not constitute substantial rights. In practice, taxpayers routinely fail IRS audits when they negotiate Fairchild-compliant acceptance and risk clauses in a Statement of Work (SOW), but execute an overarching Master Service Agreement (MSA) containing boilerplate intellectual property clauses that vest sole and exclusive ownership of all work product, designs, and technical data in the client without a royalty-free license-back.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the appellate jurisprudence of Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States and its subsequent circuit court interpretations into actionable tax and legal practice, the following two industry case studies examine realistic commercial and government-contracting scenarios. Each case study diagnoses fatal vulnerabilities that would trigger IRS disallowance under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and provides a comprehensive, step-by-step remediation blueprint across contract terms, technical documentation, project governance, and financial tracking.
Case Study 1: Aerospace and Defense Subcontractor Developing Autonomous Avionics and Thermal Propulsion Subsystems
Scenario and Pitfall Diagnosis

Apex AeroSystems Corp. ("Apex"), a United States Tier-1 aerospace and defense engineering corporation, enters into a $45,000,000 subcontract with a major defense prime contractor (operating under a Department of Defense program) to design, develop, and deliver three pre-production prototype units of an integrated, high-heat-flux thermal management and fly-by-wire autonomous avionics system. The contract is structured as a Fixed-Price Incentive (FPI) agreement with a target cost of $38,000,000, a target fee of $3,000,000, and a ceiling price of $45,000,000.

To maintain working capital during the 36-month engineering cycle, the contract provides for monthly "Milestone Progress Billings" equal to 80% of Apex's actual incurred direct labor and material costs. However, Apex's legal and tax posture suffers from four critical defects that invite immediate IRS challenge. First, regarding unconditional progress retention, the subcontract's payment clause states that monthly progress billings are invoiced and payable within 30 days based on submitted timesheets and material receipts, with no explicit contractual provision requiring Apex to refund or repay those progress payments if the final prototype fails flight-qualification testing. Second, the Statement of Work (SOW) relies on a vague effort standard rather than rigid technical pass/fail acceptance criteria, stating merely that Apex shall "utilize its best engineering efforts to design and deliver three prototype avionics suites substantially conforming to system architecture goals". Third, the contract commingles scope and accounting by failing to segregate the experimental Full-Scale Development (FSD) prototype engineering from routine post-delivery maintenance, logistics, and production tooling, grouping the entire $45,000,000 scope into a single undifferentiated contract price. Fourth, the prime contractor's standard commercial flow-down terms include a restrictive intellectual property clause stipulating that all designs, source code, schematics, and technical data developed under the subcontract shall be the sole and exclusive property of the Prime Contractor, and prohibiting Apex from utilizing or reproducing such data for any other customer without the Prime Contractor's prior written consent and a negotiated royalty.

Upon an IRS Large Business and International (LB&I) examination, the IRS engineer and trial counsel will disallow 100% of Apex's claimed QREs as "funded" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). Unlike Fairchild's refundable financing advances under DAR 7-104.35(h), Apex's monthly progress payments are non-refundable reimbursements for incurred costs; thus, under Geosyntec and Grigsby, Apex bears only cost-of-performance overrun risk above the $45,000,000 ceiling, not the risk of nonpayment upon research failure. Moreover, the "best engineering efforts" phrasing obligates the prime contractor to pay for the performance of the research rather than a successful product or result. Finally, the flow-down IP clause strips Apex of "substantial rights" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and Lockheed Martin because Apex must pay a negotiated royalty to use the research results.
Step-by-Step Remediation Blueprint
Step 1: Restructuring Contract Terms

Prior to commencing any engineering performance—thereby satisfying the upfront execution mandate of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(i) and Fairchild—Apex must execute a formal bilateral contract modification with the prime contractor restructuring four core contractual articles. First, Apex must implement strict Line-Item Segregation (CLIN Structure) by dividing the single $45,000,000 scope into eight separately priced Contract Line Items: CLINs 0001 through 0006 covering distinct FSD subsystem prototypes and environmental qualification testing totaling $36,000,000; CLIN 0007 covering production tooling for $5,000,000; and CLIN 0008 covering post-delivery field support for $4,000,000. The contract must explicitly state that Apex remains independently at financial risk for each discrete CLIN until formal acceptance of that specific line item.

Second, Apex must replace the "best engineering efforts" language with an express Total System Responsibility and Inspection, Rejection, and Cure Clause mirroring DAR 7-302.2 and DAR 7-302.4. This clause must stipulate that the Prime Contractor's obligation to pay the contract price for CLINs 0001–0006 is strictly contingent upon each prototype passing formal Acceptance Test Procedures (ATPs). If any prototype fails to meet the technical specifications, the Prime Contractor must hold the unilateral contractual right to reject the deliverable outright with zero payment liability, require Apex to re-engineer and correct the defective unit at Apex's sole expense without adjustment to the ceiling price, or accept the non-conforming unit subject to a bilateral equitable price reduction.

Third, Apex must incorporate a Refundable Financing Advance Clause mirroring DAR 7-104.35(a) and (h) that re-characterizes the monthly "Milestone Progress Billings" as "Unliquidated Financing Advances" secured by a priority security interest in Apex's work-in-process inventory. The provision must establish that Apex has no legal right to retain any financing advance unless and until the corresponding CLIN is formally delivered, tested, and accepted via a signed DD Form 250 or commercial Certificate of Conformance, at which point the advance is liquidated against the CLIN price. Crucially, the clause must include an express clawback trigger stating that if any CLIN is rejected or terminated for default due to failure to achieve technical specifications, Apex must repay 100% of all unliquidated financing advances attributable to that CLIN within 30 days of demand.

Fourth, to satisfy the substantial rights requirement under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), Apex must amend the intellectual property article to state that while the Prime Contractor receives title to the physical prototype hardware delivered under CLINs 0001–0006, Apex retains an irrevocable, perpetual, non-exclusive, worldwide, royalty-free right and license to use, modify, and exploit all underlying technical data, thermal-management algorithms, and engineering methodologies developed during the FSD phase in Apex's commercial and defense business without paying any fee or obtaining consent from the Prime Contractor.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation

To replicate the evidentiary weight of the 1,000+ pages of specifications that persuaded the Federal Circuit in Fairchild, Apex's engineering team must compile and incorporate by reference a binding System Performance and Qualification Specification Annex. This annex must establish quantitative performance barometers defining exact, objective engineering metrics required for CLIN acceptance—such as a thermal dissipation capacity of under Mach 2.5 aerodynamic heating profiles and flight-control actuator latency of under electromagnetic interference (EMI) testing per MIL-STD-461. Concurrently, for each FSD CLIN, Apex must maintain a contemporaneous Engineering Development File documenting why existing avionics cooling and control architectures cannot achieve the specification parameters (establishing technological uncertainty under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)), alongside the specific computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, breadboard iterations, and empirical test failures encountered during the process of experimentation.
Step 3: Restructuring Project Governance

Apex must institute strict internal governance controls to preserve the legal separation between risk-bearing R&D and routine contract administration. First, management must enforce a mandatory Pre-Performance Execution Gate requiring corporate tax-and-legal sign-off before opening internal R&D project charge codes, ensuring that the bilateral contract containing the contingency-of-success and advance-repayment clauses is fully executed by both parties prior to the performance of qualified research in compliance with Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(i). Second, Apex must establish formal Stage-Gate Acceptance and Non-Conformance Boards requiring that every prototype delivery be evaluated by a joint Prime-Subcontractor Test Review Board. Whenever a prototype fails an interim qualification test, the board must issue a formal Engineering Non-Conformance Report (NCR) and a Contractor Cure Directive explicitly documenting that all subsequent re-engineering, component replacement, and re-testing hours are being performed at Apex's sole financial risk pursuant to the contract's correction-of-defects clause.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation and Financial Tracking

Apex's accounting and tax departments must align the general ledger and R&D cost-accounting systems with the Federal Circuit's distinction between financing and funding. Incoming monthly 80% progress payments must not be recorded as recognized revenue upon receipt; instead, they must be booked as a current liability on Apex's balance sheet titled Unliquidated Customer Financing Advances (Refundable). These amounts should be transferred to recognized revenue (liquidated advances) strictly on a CLIN-by-CLIN basis only after the Prime Contractor executes the formal Certificate of Acceptance for that specific line item. Furthermore, Apex must implement CLIN-level cost segregation to isolate employee W-2 wages (I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)), prototype supply expenses (I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)), and third-party testing costs exclusively within the FSD line items (CLINs 0001–0006), automatically excluding all labor and materials charged to production tooling (CLIN 0007) and post-delivery support (CLIN 0008). All cost overruns above the $36,000,000 FSD target allocation must be tracked in a dedicated variance account to substantiate the real-world economic risk borne by Apex.

cells: Contractual Scope & Pricing
Single commingled $45M FPI price covering FSD prototypes, tooling, and field support.
Segregated into 8 discrete CLINs; $36M allocated across CLINs 0001–0006 for FSD prototypes with independent line-item risk.
Payment & Acceptance Standard
"Best engineering efforts" SOW; unconditional monthly progress billings tied to incurred costs.
Total System Responsibility; payment contingent on passing ATPs per DAR 7-302.2/7-302.4 equivalents; unliquidated advances refundable upon rejection per DAR 7-104.35(h).
Intellectual Property Rights
Exclusive ownership vested in Prime Contractor; royalty required for commercial reuse.
Hardware title passes to Prime, but Apex retains a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license to exploit all foreground technical data and algorithms.
Governance & Cost Accounting
Progress billings booked as revenue; commingled W-2 wage tracking across all contract tasks.
Advances booked as balance-sheet liabilities until CLIN acceptance; W-2 wages and supplies isolated to FSD CLINs 0001–0006; NCRs logged for uncompensated rework.

body.text: Case Study 2: Structural and Environmental Engineering Consultancy Designing Seismic-Resilient Industrial Infrastructure
Scenario and Pitfall Diagnosis

Vanguard Structural & Geo-Engineering LLP ("Vanguard"), a premier United States structural and environmental engineering firm, is engaged by a domestic semiconductor foundry owner ("FoundryCo") to engineer a specialized, micro-vibration-isolated subterranean foundation and an automated closed-loop chemical vapor remediation system for a new fabrication facility. Vanguard claims $1,200,000 in federal R&D tax credits based on $15,000,000 of engineering wages incurred across the project.

Vanguard operates under a commercial Capped Time-and-Materials (T&M) Agreement governed by a standard Master Services Agreement (MSA) with a maximum fee cap of $18,000,000. Vanguard's contractual and evidentiary framework exhibits the exact deficiencies that caused complete taxpayer losses in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. (MBJ) v. Commissioner (8th Cir. 2024), Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States (11th Cir. 2015), and United States v. Grigsby (5th Cir. 2023). First, Vanguard utilizes hourly invoice billing tied to its cost of performance, submitting monthly invoices based on actual engineering hours expended multiplied by scheduled hourly billing rates, plus direct expenses, up to the $18,000,000 ceiling; FoundryCo is contractually obligated to pay each monthly invoice within 30 days of receipt unless an invoice contains a clerical billing error. Second, the MSA defines Vanguard's performance obligation using a standard architectural and engineering professional standard of care rather than a result contingency, warranting only that its services "shall be performed with the degree of skill and care ordinarily exercised by reputable structural and environmental engineers practicing in the same locality under similar circumstances". Third, the contract lacks technical rejection and refund mechanics: while FoundryCo reviews schematic design (SD), design development (DD), and construction document (CD) submittals, no provision allows FoundryCo to withhold payment or demand a refund of previously paid monthly invoices if Vanguard's foundation design fails to achieve the target sub-micron vibration isolation threshold. Fourth, the MSA contains a work-for-hire intellectual property divestiture clause stating that all structural calculations, finite element models, drawings, and remediation process designs are "works made for hire" owned exclusively by FoundryCo, barring Vanguard from reusing the designs or technical data on any other project.

Under IRS examination and appellate precedent in MBJ and Geosyntec, Vanguard's research is 100% "funded" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H). As the Eleventh Circuit held in Geosyntec and the Eighth Circuit confirmed in MBJ, a capped contract where the engineer is paid via periodic invoices for work performed—even if the research fails to yield the desired technical outcome for the client—places the financial risk of failed research on the client, not the engineer. Vanguard's risk that its engineering hours might exceed the $18,000,000 cap is mere "cost-of-performance" risk, which does not satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1). Furthermore, the lack of specific technical acceptance barometers (contrasted with Fairchild and Populous Holdings) and the complete divestiture of substantial rights under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) invalidate the claim.
Step-by-Step Remediation Blueprint
Step 1: Restructuring Contract Terms

To transform its commercial arrangement from a funded services agreement into an un-funded, risk-bearing deliverable contract that satisfies Fairchild and Populous Holdings, Vanguard must eliminate the Capped T&M structure and amend the MSA and SOW prior to initiating design work. First, Vanguard must convert the pricing model from Capped T&M to Deliverable-Contingent Fixed-Price Phases, eliminating hourly time-and-materials billing entirely. The $18,000,000 contract should be divided into four discrete, fixed-priced deliverable line items: Line Item 1 covering the Subterranean Seismic and Micro-Vibration Isolation Basis of Design and Finite Element Validation ($4,500,000); Line Item 2 covering the Closed-Loop Vapor Remediation Pilot Process Design and Mass-Balance Simulation ($4,500,000); Line Item 3 covering Integrated Structural and Process Construction Documents ($6,000,000); and Line Item 4 covering Construction Administration and Field Verification ($3,000,000).

Second, Vanguard must replace the "ordinary professional skill and care" warranty in the SOW with an explicit Result-Contingent Payment and Rejection Clause. The contract must specify that FoundryCo is paying strictly for a conforming engineering work product and technical result, not for engineering hours rendered. The clause must establish that FoundryCo has no legal obligation to pay the fixed price for Line Items 1, 2, or 3 unless the engineering designs demonstrably satisfy the quantitative performance criteria in the Technical Specification Schedule. Furthermore, FoundryCo must be granted the explicit contractual right to reject any design package that fails independent peer-review validation or pilot simulation, require Vanguard to completely redesign the failed engineering package at Vanguard's sole cost without additional compensation, or terminate the contract for default.

Third, if Vanguard requires interim monthly cash draws during the performance of Line Items 1 through 3, the payment schedule must incorporate a Refundable Progress Draw Provision stipulating that all interim draws are conditional, unliquidated advances against the final fixed price of that specific Line Item. The contract must include an unequivocal refund covenant stating that if Vanguard fails to deliver a design package for any Line Item that satisfies the Acceptance Criteria set forth in Exhibit B, or if FoundryCo rejects such Line Item for failure to meet technical specifications, Vanguard shall refund to FoundryCo 100% of all interim progress draws previously paid for such Line Item within 30 days of written rejection.

Fourth, Vanguard must execute a License-Back of Substantial Rights by amending the MSA's intellectual property clause to distinguish between client-specific facility blueprints and underlying engineering innovations. The revised clause must provide that while FoundryCo owns the physical blueprints for its specific semiconductor facility, Vanguard retains full ownership—or an irrevocable, perpetual, royalty-free right and license—to use, reproduce, and commercialize all underlying seismic dampening methodologies, finite element modeling routines, and chemical remediation process algorithms developed during the project for future clients without paying any fee or royalty to FoundryCo.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation

To overcome the MBJ deficiency where contracts lacked objective technical barometers, Vanguard must attach a binding Exhibit B: Technical Performance Specifications and Acceptance Testing Protocol to the SOW. This exhibit must establish objective engineering barometers for success that govern the formal acceptance of each Line Item. Specifically, Line Item 1 must require verified three-dimensional finite element structural modeling demonstrating floor vibration velocity of (satisfying the VC-E vibration criterion curve) under a simulated 0.6g Peak Ground Acceleration seismic event, while Line Item 2 must require pilot-scale mass-transfer validation demonstrating volatile organic compound (VOC) abatement efficiency at airflow without thermal runaway. Additionally, Exhibit B must detail the formal inspection and evaluation mechanism that FoundryCo and its third-party Commissioning Authority will utilize to test, verify, and formally accept or reject each engineering submittal package.
Step 3: Restructuring Project Governance

Vanguard must enforce rigorous project governance to ensure its day-to-day operational conduct matches the contract's legal allocation of risk. Project management must be prohibited from treating routine client design review meetings as informal sign-offs; instead, Vanguard must require FoundryCo's Vice President of Facilities Engineering to execute a formal Line-Item Technical Acceptance Certificate verifying that all Exhibit B performance barometers have been satisfied before any fixed-price phase is closed or any interim progress draw is liquidated. Whenever FoundryCo or the Commissioning Authority identifies a technical failure during design review—such as a structural resonance failure in the foundation slab model—the governance protocol must mandate the issuance of a formal Notice of Technical Rejection and Cure Demand. Vanguard's principal engineer must then log a formal corrective action plan documenting that the subsequent redesign iterations were mandated and performed at Vanguard's sole financial risk.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation and Financial Tracking

Vanguard must overhaul its timekeeping and accounting systems to substantiate both the four-part test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1) and the financial risk rules of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). Generic phase-level time billing (such as "Schematic Design - 40 hours") must be replaced with granular, contemporaneous, activity-based time-tracking codes tied directly to the iterative process of experimentation for Line Items 1 and 2 (for example, LI-01.3: Iterative ANSYS Dynamic Soil-Structure Interaction Modeling to resolve VC-E vibration uncertainty), while all hours spent on Line Item 4 (Construction Administration) and routine building-code compliance checks must be excluded from the QRE pool. In Vanguard's general ledger, all labor costs incurred on Line Items 1, 2, and 3 must be segregated into an At-Risk Work-in-Process (WIP) asset account, and any interim cash draws must be recorded in a Conditional Client Advances (Subject to Technical Acceptance Refund) liability account. Revenue recognition and advance liquidation may occur strictly upon receipt of the signed Line-Item Technical Acceptance Certificate, and all unbilled rework hours incurred during technical rejection cycles must be tracked in a separate job-cost sub-ledger to provide irrefutable audit proof that Vanguard bore the financial burden of failed research steps.

cells: Contractual Billing & Risk Model
$18M Capped T&M contract billed monthly via hourly invoices; exposes firm only to cost-of-performance risk.
Converted into 4 fixed-price deliverable Line Items; interim draws structured as conditional advances subject to a 100% refund clawback upon rejection.
Performance Standard & Barometers
Standard professional skill and care warranty; routine client design reviews without strict pass/fail barometers.
Result-contingent acceptance tied to Exhibit B quantitative metrics ( VC-E vibration; VOC abatement) and formal inspection.
Intellectual Property Rights
"Work made for hire" MSA vesting exclusive ownership of all models and designs in FoundryCo.
FoundryCo owns facility blueprints, while Vanguard retains a perpetual, royalty-free license to exploit all underlying structural and process methodologies.
Governance & Time/Cost Tracking
Generic phase-level timecards; monthly invoices booked immediately as revenue.
Activity-based experimentation time codes; WIP asset and Conditional Advance liability accounting until formal Line-Item Acceptance Certificate execution.

metaDescription: Fairchild Industries v. United States (Fed. Cir. 1995): research is not “funded” when payment is contingent on technical success and acceptance.
